messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Kofi presents as a poised and articulate 22-year-old, a man who has achieved the position of School Principal at an age when most of his peers are just beginning their careers. Yet, beneath the calm exterior he projects to his staff and students, he carries a profound and unyielding terror. The trauma dates back to his childhood, to a time spent in the care of an uncle whose moods were a volatile, unpredictable force. Kofi’s attempts to deliberately recall the specifics of those years are met with a frustrating fog. When he tries to construct a linear narrative, the memories refuse to cohere. Instead, they surface as fragmented pieces: the sharp, metallic click of a belt buckle, the scent of rain on hot asphalt outside a window he wasn't allowed to open, the specific floral pattern on a couch cushion pressed against his cheek. These sensory snapshots arrive without warning and feel, as he describes it, more real and vivid than his memory of his own college graduation. The past feels more present than the present.

The echoes of his uncle's unpredictability reverberate through his daily life at the school. Last week, a fire alarm was pulled as a prank, and the sudden, unscheduled chaos of evacuating the building sent a jolt of panic through him that was entirely out of proportion. He felt a familiar, cold dread, the same feeling he’d had as a boy when his uncle’s laughter would curdle into rage for no discernible reason. In these moments, Kofi feels a terrifying helplessness, a deep-seated conviction that he can't stop bad things from happening. This belief shadows him, turning minor administrative hurdles into proof of his powerlessness. It is in these moments of perceived chaos that his greatest fear emerges. He feels a surge of hot anger rising in his chest, a mirror of the rage he once endured. He is certain that if he were to let it out, he would not be able to control his anger and would do something terrible, perhaps to a child who was misbehaving. The thought is so abhorrent that he physically recoils, clenching his fists until his knuckles are white to keep the feeling contained.

This internal battle has led to a slow retreat from his life. His girlfriend, Amara, recently bought a beautiful silver frame, wanting to put a favorite photo of them on the mantelpiece. Kofi found himself making excuses, unable to look at the image of their shared happiness without a wave of anxiety. Old photos of any kind feel dangerous, like portals to a past he cannot manage. He has also begun avoiding direct disciplinary actions with students, delegating them to his vice-principal. He frames it as empowerment, but knows he is running from the possibility of an unpredictable confrontation that could unleash the rage he is so terrified of. This has started to cause a quiet friction with his staff, who perceive him as increasingly distant. Even sleep offers no escape. He often wakes from nightmares, the residue of fear clinging to him like a damp shroud, making him irritable and detached for hours. Waking up next to Amara, he feels a profound sense of alienation, as if he is a damaged object that doesn't belong in her world of gentle normalcy.

He has come to believe that the abuse has permanently changed him for the worse, that some essential part of his character was broken and can never be repaired. His professional success feels like a fragile costume, and he lives in constant fear of being exposed as the broken, helpless boy he still feels he is. It was an incident two weeks ago that finally compelled him to seek help. A student had defiantly sworn at him in the hallway, and for a terrifying second, Kofi saw his uncle’s face superimposed on the child’s. The impulse to lash out was so overwhelming that he had to turn and walk away without a word, leaving a stunned silence behind him. He spent the rest of the day locked in his office, shaking. The fear of becoming the man who hurt him is now greater than the fear of the memories themselves, and he is desperate to find a way to believe he is not destined to repeat the past.
